summary: Describes alternate and additional mechanisms for MPLS-TP linear protection beyond those in RFC 6378, so that operators get behavior closer to what they know from SDH, OTN, and Ethernet transport networks. It introduces capabilities and modes, namely PSC mode and APS mode, and updates RFC 6378.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds five optional behaviors to MPLS-TP linear protection. Endpoints report which behaviors they use, and they stop protection switching if their capability settings do not match.

questions: what is the difference between psc mode and aps mode
what is the mpls-tp ms-w command
subtitle: Adds MPLS-TP protection-switching behavior that matches expectations from other transport networks.

tldr.problem: The original MPLS-TP protection protocol handles some priorities and commands differently from other transport networks.
tldr.mechanism: Five capabilities change priority handling, non-revertive behavior, manual switching, Signal Degrade protection and the Exercise command. A Capabilities TLV reports the selected mode.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines PSC and APS modes and updates RFC 6378. RFC 8234 later updates it.

today: RFC 7271 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6378 and is updated by RFC 8234.

sections.title: Why Add Protection Capabilities
sections.content:
RFC 6378 defines linear protection for MPLS-TP. This document adds alternate and additional mechanisms intended to give operators behavior closer to linear protection in SDH, OTN and Ethernet transport networks.

The five capabilities cover request priorities, non-revertive behavior, the MS-W command, Signal Degrade protection and the EXER command. A mode is a particular set of capabilities; this RFC defines PSC mode and APS mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Two paths can protect a transport service when one path fails. This RFC adds control choices to make the switching behavior more familiar to transport operators.

sections.title: Changing Request Priorities
sections.content:
The priority-modification capability raises Signal Fail on the Protection path above Forced Switch and raises Clear Signal Fail. Under the earlier priority order, a protection-path failure could interrupt service or leave the endpoints with different path selections.

The capability also adds a local Freeze command. Freeze blocks local commands, condition changes and received PSC information until it is cleared. Because Freeze is not sent to the peer, using it at only one end can cause protocol failure.
sections.plainLanguage: A failure on the backup path must not be overridden by a request to switch onto it. The revised priority order helps the two ends keep traffic on a usable path.

sections.title: Non-Revertive Operation and Manual Switches
sections.content:
The non-revertive capability enters Do-not-Revert when an operator clears a switch-over command, not only when a fault clears. The MS-W command lets an operator move traffic back to the working path from that state without first locking out the protection path.

MS-P and MS-W have equal priority. When opposite commands arrive simultaneously, MS-W wins and MS-P is cancelled. The Request and Fault Path fields identify the command and the path from which traffic is diverted.
sections.plainLanguage: Non-revertive operation keeps traffic on the selected path after a request ends. MS-W adds a direct command for moving traffic back to the working path.

sections.title: Signal Degrade and Exercise
sections.content:
The Signal Degrade capability applies protection switching to degraded signal conditions; the method for detecting degradation is outside this RFC. When degradation exists on either path, the node duplicates user traffic onto both paths. In revertive mode, duplication continues through the Wait-to-Restore state.

EXER tests PSC communication and the protection path without switching traffic. A node receiving EXER should answer with Reverse Request. If both ends issue EXER at once, a node that receives EXER before Reverse Request treats it as Reverse Request.
sections.plainLanguage: A degraded path can trigger traffic duplication across both paths while the problem remains. EXER checks the protection signaling without moving user traffic.

sections.title: Capabilities and Modes
sections.content:
Each PSC message carries a Capabilities TLV with flag bits that describe the sender's selected behaviors. Type 1 identifies this TLV. A sender must include its capabilities in every PSC message and set unused bits to zero.

Receiving endpoints compare the flag values. If they differ, the endpoint must alert the operator and stop protection switching until the mismatch is resolved. PSC mode uses no new capabilities; APS mode uses all five and has flag value 0xF8000000.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint reports its capability settings in PSC messages. If the reports differ, both need an operator to resolve the mismatch before switching traffic.

sections.title: Mismatches, Security and Registry Values
sections.content:
In APS mode, some path or protection-type mismatches require an alert and a pause in switching. A mismatch in the Capabilities TLV has the same effect. A data-path mismatch lasting more than 50 ms may be reported while switching continues; missing protection-path messages can require switching to stop.

The RFC says it introduces no new security risks and refers to RFC 6378 and RFC 5920. IANA assigned Request values 2 for Reverse Request and 3 for Exercise, plus a Capabilities TLV type and flag registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Some configuration disagreements require switching to pause until an operator fixes them. The RFC also assigns shared code values for the new messages and capability flags.
